I've been farming these 7 mu in Quzhou for over forty years, and at sixty-two I'm not about to start experimenting. Wheat and corn have always fed my family, and that's what I'll stick with. Last year the wheat gave me about 460 jin per mu and the corn did a bit better, around 500 jin. Not great, not terrible — enough to live on and sell a little.

This year I'll plant improved wheat seed — probably something like Shimai or Liangxing, whatever the seed station has that my neighbors say worked well — on all 7 mu in mid-October. The extension fellow tells me 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is plenty, but I've always put down closer to 18 kg. I use a compound fertilizer as base, about 50 kg per mu, then topdress with urea at green-up and jointing. Better to spend a bit more than risk the wheat turning yellow. I'll run the rotary tiller before sowing because the soil gets hard after the summer. For water, I'll irrigate four times: once before winter freeze-up, once when the wheat wakes up in spring, once at jointing, and once at heading. The pump electricity isn't cheap, but dry wheat is worthless. I'll spray three times — herbicide once, then insecticide and fungicide when I see problems.

Come June, as soon as the wheat is off, I'll plant hybrid corn straight in with no-till. There's no time to plough — the window is barely a week, and anyway the less I disturb the soil the better. I'll put down about 15 kg N per mu, plus some phosphorus and potassium in the compound fertilizer at planting. The corn only needs two good irrigations, one at the V6 stage and one at tasseling, if the rains don't come. Three sprays should handle the weeds and the borers. I thought about cotton, but my back hurts enough already at harvest time, and the corn can be combined. I'll aim for 480 kg per mu on the wheat and 520 on the corn. That's realistic — not greedy, not lazy. Just what the land usually gives me if I do my part.
